Millard Creek and its main tributary Piercy Creek flow through rural and urban areas where they are exposed to impacts from human activities. Millard Piercy Watershed Stewards have been collecting water quality data at 12 locations throughout the watershed for more than 20 years.  The objective is to establish long term trends and to identify point source pollution. The data are reported to the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, and violations of the habitat protection provisions or the Fisheries Act are reported to the respective authorities. The water quality measuring instruments are old with some suspicious measurements. Maintenance and calibration attempts have failed to solve the problem.  This grant will provide acquisition of hardware to ensure that the data are correct and meet scientific standards. This will support informed decisions regarding a sustainable water management in favour of the health of humans and life in the watershed with focus on salmon populations.

Green Ummah is a Canadian non-profit that aims to raise environmental and social justice awareness within the Muslim community. Founded by youth advocates, it has grown to include a diverse team and volunteer base. In partnership with Nature Canada, the organization has hosted Canada's first Muslim-organized environmental conference and developed the Greening our Communities Toolkit, a curriculum focused on environmental justice. Initially launched in five classes, the toolkit has expanded to 25, reaching beyond the Muslim community to engage racialized and newcomer students. The program has revealed a high demand for education on environmental racism in Ontario schools and uncovered a lack of nature engagement among marginalized students. The grant will fund curriculum updates, teacher training, and program expansion.

A la Baie Metis Local 21 leads the Sakitawak Indigenous Protected and Conserved Area project in Ile a La Crosse, focusing on conserving local ecosystems like forests, freshwater, and peat. A key aim is to protect the Woodland Caribou in the Pine River Valley. The project, guided by a ten-year strategic plan, incorporates local assets, ecotourism models, and long-standing Indigenous knowledge. In partnership with Nature Canada, it seeks to identify priority areas for caribou habitat restoration, provide technical advice for caribou restoration, and empower community-led reforestation efforts. The grant will help develop a conservation plan and outreach materials to further these objectives.

The Alliance of Canadian Land Trusts (ACLT) is focused on advancing land conservation across Canada through a multi-pronged approach. Key initiatives include the development of outreach materials, such as a comprehensive guide aimed at aiding municipalities and land trusts in conservation efforts. ACLT also works on Municipal Assessment Reports, aimed at standardizing conservation practices, and researches mapping tools to identify current and potential municipal conserved areas. A significant project involves compiling a national database of land trusts and their areas of operation. This database will serve as a cornerstone for future conservation initiatives, facilitating collaborations with provincial bodies and Indigenous groups. ACLT plans to conduct surveys and information-gathering projects to identify existing partnerships between land trusts and municipalities. The purpose of this grant is to fulfill several needs in Kathmandu, Nepal. It aims to relieve poverty by providing essential humanitarian assistance to individuals in need. Additionally, it seeks to offer comprehensive support, including counselling, education, food, clothing, and shelter, to those affected by violence and human trafficking. Another fulfilled need is to advance education by offering scholarships, bursaries, awards, and other forms of financial assistance to students in need, enabling them to attend schools, colleges, and universities that provide degree courses and trades programs. The grant also focuses on developing and implementing educational programs designed to raise awareness about human trafficking and offer effective prevention strategies. It provides vocational training programs that equip individuals with skills for long-term employment. Lastly, we collaborate with local organizations to create sustainable solutions for preventing human trafficking.

purpose: To develop a training course to help people living with Type 1 Diabetes to improve their mental wellbeing in relation to managing their condition.

Contributions to JDRF T1D Fund, LLC which is based in the US. The T1D fund was formed solely for charitable purposes to materially accelerate research and development of new, life changing breakthroughs that have the potential of providing a cure, prevention and treatment of Type 1 Diabetes and its complications. Management of a venture philanthropy fund by using donations and our T1D scientific expertise to encourage more venture capital, biotech and pharma investments to accelerate research to cure T1D.

Funding a research project in Israel to do nationwide childhood Type 1 diabetes (T1D) screening. Co-hosted by Ochapowace First Nation and Chacachas First Nation within the boundaries of the Archdiocese of Regina.  The project is a 3 day camp led by IRS survivors and youth from Ochapowace and Chacachas First Nations. Participants from include 120+ high school youth/parents/survivors (Elders and Knowledge Keepers) from six nearby First Nations' schools/communities and non-Indigenous students/parents from Whitewood high school community will participate learning and walking together in the spirit of reconciliation.  The first day explores the history of colonization, the Indian Act, residential schools, harmful intergenerational impacts, and Treaty 4 promises. The second day features learning about decolonization by exploring pre-contact Cree Natural Laws and teachings focusing on leadership principles and values that can be used. The  third day, is a reflection on how they can walk in both two worlds using the best of Indigenous and non-Indigenous ways of knowing and doing.

recipient_name: Kici-Anishnabek Kananakachiwewat Community Cote Culture Camp
purpose: Implements TRC healing between Church and Cote FN. Between July 23 and 28, 2023, the Cote First Nation Elders will offer a culture camp which will bring together Elders from the community with the youth and children from the area. The 5-day camp will focus on teaching and learning land-based survival skills together with Onakawek language skills. For some time signs of some dysfunction in the community (drug and substance abuse, suicide, lack of respect and disengagement) it was decided to offer a summer Youth Culture Camp with the following goals: a) Teach traditional First Nations land-based and language skills; b) Build a positive experience in participants in learning basic traditions in understanding their past; c) Build self-awareness and self-esteem through completion of successful activities; d) Help participants to identify ways to use newly acquired skills in the community; and e) Show parents and community members that the camp is a positive experience for their youth.

To enable a Woodland Cree traditional Moose hide tanning camp. This Culture camp will also include netting for fish  cleaning fish  and smoking and frying fish for lunch and supper. Participants will also learn how to cut and smoke moose meat for preservation and consumption The fish will be distributed to the community elders and low-income families. Birds Culture Camp has very knowledgeable elders who take these teachings with pride and are very keen on passing down the knowledge to the next generation. This grant will help ensure that each student is impacted by these teachings.

Green Ummah is a Canadian non-profit that aims to raise environmental and social justice awareness within the Muslim community. Founded by youth advocates  it has grown to include a diverse team and volunteer base. In partnership with Nature Canada  the organization has hosted Canada's first Muslim-organized environmental conference and developed the 'Greening our Communities Toolkit ' a curriculum focused on environmental justice. Initially launched in five classes  the toolkit has expanded to 25  reaching beyond the Muslim community to engage racialized and newcomer students. The program has revealed a high demand for education on environmental racism in Ontario schools and uncovered a lack of nature engagement among marginalized students. The grant will fund curriculum updates  teacher training  and program expansion.

Distribution of 1050 care packages for unhoused community members in collaboration with students from Comox Valley schools. Care packages include homemade holiday cards  cookies  warm socks  toques  mitts  scarves and toiletries. Participating students learn about community leadership  rehumanizing homelessness  addiction  compassion  local poverty  project management  marketing  self-care in service  gratitude and being changemakers. Care packages were distributed at 16 local Comox Valley support agencies  shelters and soup kitchens.

Funding for direct support services for Indigenous people who are unhoused or at risk of unhoused. Current client base is the urban Indigenous population with an emphasis on women  youth  and two spirit individuals. The majority of these clients are living in Courtenay's downtown core. Support services include advocacy  assisting with housing searches/applications and support with maintaining housing. A portion of this funding was also used for emergency needs for unhoused individuals such as equipment (tents  sleeping bags  hygiene  etc)  and transportation needs.

Funding for weekly meal service on Sundays in the Comox Valley  serving 70+ clients a week. The unhoused population relies on the meal program on Sundays to ensure they are fed a well nutritious and consistent meal. Clients can also access harm reduction supplies  donated clothing items  water  naloxone training  blankets  toiletries  tents and blankets. The unhoused community thrives off the connection with others at this program  and it helps to encourage the use of resources within the Comox Valley. Funding is primarily for food costs as well as program expenses.

Address food sovereignty and food security issues  and Food First NL s new province-wide Lived/Living Experience Advisory Group  This grant will empower individuals facing food insecurity with knowledge of how the emergency food system operates  how it could be better  and the tools to engage with it. This project aligns with Food First NL s overall approach to educational and outreach initiatives  which is focused on creating space for and valuing community-level insights into our food system as a way of enabling action. They have a long history of leading community-led food assessments  hosting hands-on food skills workshops  and creating opportunities for intergenerational learning around food.

This project will build community-based infrastructure to make fresh  local food more accessible in Newfoundland and Labrador particularly in rural communities  where barriers to food access are at their highest.  Many Newfoundlanders and Labradorians  particularly rural ones  face geographical and logistical barriers to accessing the food they would like to eat. Even with adequate income  food access can be very limited for people who don t have access to a vehicle or to the very substantial time and money needed to travel to a large centre. Access to the freshest local food is often even more difficult  with a distributed and often difficult-to-find network of producers.

Building on already-approved funding from the Government of NL  this grant will enable Food First NL to lead a comprehensive and collaborative consultation process that will inform recommendations for the timely roll-out of a universal school food program in Newfoundland and Labrador. It will also allow Food First NL to fully participate in school food advocacy  programming  and funding efforts led by national partners  building capacity and connections more broadly for Newfoundland and Labrador.

The Consecon Foundation made 5 grants  totalling $167 766 ($10 000 in Jan 2024  $15 000 in Feb 2024  $50 000 in Aug 2024  $50 000 in Aug 2024  and $42 766 in Dec 2024).   The Jan and Feb grants facilitated a strategic planning exercise in Montreal  including a tour of a cell culture manufacturing facility and a networking event for the Montreal cellular agriculture community.  The grants in Aug 2024 were the interim and final payments for a grant agreement signed in Dec 2023  to -Support Cellular Agriculture Canada (CAC) activities and costs associated with the organization -Convene meetings with provincial and federal officials and other parties -Prepare other funding proposals and support cellular agriculture research  The Dec 2024 grant covered strategic planning and community building work in Edmonton in September 2024  including: the second gathering of CAC  and an international conference bringing together 20 international leaders in cellular agriculture.

The Consecon Foundation made a three-year  $150 000 funding commitment to Ontario Genomics to support cellular agriculture initiatives in Ontario from 2024-26. We believe Ontario Genomics' work will help Canada create a more sustainable food system  which will support the foundation's work in one of its key program areas: accelerating the protein transition.   The first year of the program focused on the development & preparation of a follow-up report to Ontario Genomics' groundbreaking 2021 report on cellular agriculture in Canada. The grant supported research for the revised report as well as costs of report launch and communications. The report was launched in March 2025 and can be found here: https://www.ontariogenomics.ca/canada-synbio-2024-unlocking-the-future/  The foundation also made a grant of $10 000 to support Ontario Genomics' Canada Synbio 2024 conference. Volunteers from the Emmaus Community and Abbey Church participate in this program. Participant feedback highlighted the vital role the program played in alleviating food insecurity  especially amid rising grocery costs. Many respondents described the hampers as  immensely helpful  noting the positive impact on both nutrition and mental wellbeing.   The program also fostered meaningful collaboration between local organizations and the business community  strengthening neighbourhood-level relationships.
